Fit a Bayesian spatial regression with a 2D Gaussian Process (via brms)

Source: R/model-bayesian.R
fit_bayesian_spatial_model.Rd

Fits a regression whose residual spatial structure is modelled explicitly, as a Gaussian process over the coordinates, and so kept out of the errors. Two things follow, and they are the reasons to reach for this backend. First, every quantity comes with a posterior, so predictions carry intervals instead of point estimates. Whether those intervals are calibrated is something to measure, not assume: score them with cv_bayes(), which reports held-out interval coverage and CRPS. Second, the spatial term is a smooth regional surface at a stated resolution. The Gaussian process is fitted through a reduced-rank basis, and that basis has a floor: an effective range below which it cannot represent structure, reported in map units as $info$gp_resolution and by print(). With the defaults the floor is 14 to 33 percent of the extent along each axis (about 32 km on a uniform 100 km square, 155 km east-west and 63 km north-south on the census tracts of North Carolina). Structure shorter than the floor is counted as noise: the fitted range comes out too long, the residual standard deviation too large, and the intervals too narrow where the structure is. See "What the basis resolves" below.

Usage

fit_bayesian_spatial_model(
  data_sf,
  response_var,
  predictor_vars,
  family = NULL,
  gp_k = NULL,
  gp_c = NULL,
  gp_iso = FALSE,
  prior = NULL,
  chains = 4,
  iter = 2000,
  warmup = floor(iter/2),
  cores = getOption("mc.cores", 1L),
  seed = 123,
  backend = c("auto", "cmdstanr", "rstan"),
  control = list(),
  compute_loo = TRUE,
  standardize_predictors = FALSE,
  check_convergence = TRUE,
  pointize = "auto",
  boundary = NULL,
  gp_resolution = NULL,
  .already_prepped = FALSE
)

Arguments

data_sf

An sf object with response, predictors, and geometries.

response_var

Response column name.

predictor_vars

Predictor column names. May be character(0) for an intercept-only model: the response is then explained by the intercept and the spatial Gaussian process alone, which is the right baseline for asking how much of the surface is spatial structure and how much covariate effect (and the natural null model for comparing against a covariate model with compare_models).

family

A model family accepted by brms::brm(): a stats family function such as poisson(), or a brms family object such as brms::zero_inflated_poisson(), brms::negbinomial(), brms::hurdle_poisson(), brms::bernoulli() or brms::Beta(). Default NULL, resolved to stats::gaussian(). The family reaches brms::brm() unchanged with the spatial GP term still in the formula. A factor response is accepted only under brms::categorical() or an ordinal family, and those fits have no single expected value per row, so several methods cannot use them; see the section on non-Gaussian responses for what each family supports, and the count example below.

gp_k

Positive integer giving the number of GP basis functions per dimension, or NULL (default) to derive it from the length-scale/domain ratio. The fitted model carries gp_k^2 basis functions, not gp_k (see Details). A value above the derived one makes the basis finer, and the length-scale prior's lower tail moves down to the length-scale that basis resolves, because a finer basis under the default prior gains almost nothing. A value below the derived one leaves the prior where it was, mostly below what the basis resolves; that share is stored as $info$gp_adequacy$prior_mass_below, logged when it passes 10 percent and flagged by print(). To ask for a resolution in map units, use gp_resolution and leave this NULL.

gp_c

Positive numeric boundary factor for the approximate GP, or NULL (default) to derive it alongside gp_k. The boundary must be wide enough to contain the longest plausible correlation range; a value that is too small truncates the domain and degrades the approximation for smooth, long-range surfaces. When you set gp_c and leave gp_k = NULL, gp_k is derived for your boundary: a wider boundary needs more basis functions to resolve the same length-scale, so raising gp_c raises the derived gp_k with it, up to the cap of 50 per dimension (a capped value is logged).

gp_iso

Logical; passed to brms::gp(iso = ). FALSE (the default) fits a separate length-scale per coordinate axis, letting the model learn any directional structure from the data. TRUE fits a single shared length-scale, which makes the kernel anisotropic in the original CRS by whatever ratio sd(X)/sd(Y) happens to take, because the coordinates are standardised per axis beforehand. See Details.

prior

Optional brms prior specification. When NULL and standardize_predictors = TRUE, a weakly informative prior is set on the regression coefficients, on the scale of the linear predictor: normal(0, 2.5 * sd(y)) under an identity link (gaussian, student, skew-normal and mixtures of them), normal(0, 2.5 * sd(log(y))) for the lognormal families, whose location is on the log scale, and the fixed normal(0, 5) under any other link (log, logit and so on), where the linear predictor has a scale of its own. sd() is taken over the training rows. The result therefore does not depend on the units of the response: a fixed normal(0, 5) under an identity link, which is what earlier versions set, left a slope alone when income was in thousands of dollars and shrank the same slope to nothing when it was in dollars. The prior brms used is stored as $info$b_prior and shown by print(). When prior is given, no slope prior is added. A data-informed GP length-scale prior is always appended automatically unless prior already contains an entry with class = "lscale".

chains

Number of MCMC chains. Default 4.

iter

Total iterations per chain. Default 2000.

warmup

Warmup iterations. Default floor(iter/2).

cores

Number of cores for the sampler, one chain per core. Default getOption("mc.cores", 1L), the same convention brms uses itself, so options(mc.cores = 4) once per session runs the four default chains in parallel everywhere. The previous default of detectCores() - 1 took every core but one on any machine, which is not what a shared server or a check farm wants.

seed

Integer seed. Default 123.

backend

"auto" (default), "cmdstanr", or "rstan". "auto" uses cmdstanr only when a CmdStan build is actually available, and rstan otherwise, which brms always brings. The cmdstanr package is a thin interface and can be installed without a CmdStan build (cmdstanr::install_cmdstan() builds one). An explicit "cmdstanr" with no usable CmdStan raises an error that says how to install it, so the failure does not come from inside the sampler.

control

Named list of sampler controls, merged over the package defaults list(adapt_delta = 0.9, max_treedepth = 12) instead of replacing them. Passing list(max_treedepth = 15) therefore keeps adapt_delta = 0.9, which matters, because that is exactly the setting the divergence warning tells you to raise.

compute_loo

Logical; compute PSIS-LOO. Default TRUE.

standardize_predictors

Logical; center and scale numeric predictors before fitting. Default FALSE. When TRUE, the scaling parameters are stored in the return value ($info$predictor_scaling, a center and scale per predictor) so predictions can be computed correctly. The model is then fitted on the standardised predictors, so coef() reports a slope per standard deviation of each predictor and an intercept at the predictor means, not the raw-unit values stats::lm() would give; see coef.bayesian_fit.

check_convergence

Logical; after fitting, read the sampler's diagnostics and set $info$convergence_ok. The verdict follows Stan's own diagnostics, with these thresholds:

  • any divergent transition after warmup;

  • bulk or tail effective sample size below 100 per chain for any parameter (Vehtari et al. 2021; the rule rstan warns on). It is an absolute count: a share of the draws, which earlier versions used, asks for 100 in all at chains = 2, iter = 1000;

  • rank-normalised split R-hat, in two tiers. Above 1.05, the value rstan's own sampler warning uses, for any parameter. Above 1.01, the value Vehtari et al. (2021) recommend, for a parameter whose effective sample size is also below the count in the previous item, or cannot be read;

  • E-BFMI below 0.3 in any chain (Betancourt 2016).

An R-hat between 1.01 and 1.05 on a parameter with enough effective draws is a caution, not a failure: it is stored by name in $info$convergence_diagnostics$rhat_caution, logged, and counted by print(). The reason is the number of parameters. This model has one weight per basis function, about 540 parameters at the usual basis, and the largest of that many R-hat values sits near 1.01 in a fit that has converged: four fits at the default four chains of 2,000 iterations had largest values of 1.005, 1.009, 1.009 and 1.011, with every effective sample size at least 1,086 against the 400 required. Chains that have converged by construction (540 independent parameters, four chains of 1,000 draws) had a largest value of 1.008 to 1.011 at an effective sample size near 1,300, and 130 to 160 values above 1.01, none above 1.05, at an effective sample size near 450. Vehtari et al. give 1.01 beside an effective sample size above 400, and an R-hat of 1.01 is about what an effective sample size of 400 gives (1.009 on average in the same chains), so the two are read together here.

Transitions that stop at max_treedepth are counted and logged but do not change the verdict: Stan treats them as a cost, not as invalid draws. A failed verdict sets convergence_ok to FALSE, raises one R warning of class spatialkit_convergence naming each failed check with its count and its first five parameters, and print() flags it; $info$convergence_diagnostics holds every value. The warning closes with the remedy for the checks that failed: a higher adapt_delta for divergent transitions, which more iterations do not remove, and more iterations for R-hat and effective sample size. cv_bayes() marks such folds in fold_metrics$convergence_ok and compare_models() names such a model. A short run usually fails, on effective sample size: two fits of two chains and 300 post-warmup draws each had two or three parameters below 100 effective draws per chain, and 66 and 76 of their 537 parameters above R-hat 1.01.

The same step checks the GP basis against the posterior and the residuals (see "What the basis resolves") and stores the result as $info$gp_adequacy. The residuals need the fitted values, one pass over the posterior that fitted() caches for later calls. That check is about the approximation, not the sampler, so it does not change convergence_ok; print() and summary() show its status, and two of its states raise a warning of class spatialkit_gp_adequacy. FALSE skips all of these and leaves convergence_ok NA (not checked) and the adequacy status "not_checked". Default TRUE.

pointize

Strategy for non-point geometry coercion.

boundary

Optional polygonal sf/sfc whose CRS the data are projected to. It is not a clip: rows outside it are kept.

gp_resolution

The shortest effective range the basis should resolve, as a single positive number in the units of the data's CRS (metres for a UTM layer), or NULL (default) for the percentile rule described under Details. gp_k is derived from it, and the length-scale prior's lower tail moves with the basis. It can only refine: a value the default basis already resolves leaves the default basis in place. It is an error when the basis it needs exceeds the cap of 50 functions per dimension (2,500 in all); the message gives the basis size needed and the shortest range the cap reaches on this layout. Cost grows with gp_k^2. Give gp_resolution or gp_k, not both.

.already_prepped

Logical (internal). If TRUE, skip the prep_model_data() call because the caller has already projected, coerced, and filtered the data. The data must then have plain POINT geometry (an error is raised otherwise). Used by the CV internals to avoid a redundant second pass on every fold. End users should leave this at the default FALSE.

Value

A bayesian_fit object (inherits from spatial_fit). Supports predict(), fitted(), residuals(), coef(), summary(), and model_metrics(). Model-specific metadata lives in $info (coords: the names of the scaled coordinate columns handed to brms::gp(); coord_scaling, predictor_scaling, gp_k, gp_c, gp_iso, gp_n_basis, gp_ell_min, gp_resolution: the smallest effective range the basis resolves, as c(x, y) in map units; gp_resolution_requested: the gp_resolution argument, or NULL; gp_prefit: the check made before sampling, a list with status ("ok"; "below_floor", the one that warns; "below_floor_no_autocorrelation" and "below_floor_long_range", a range below the floor that the short-lag or the floor-distance test did not bear out; "not_estimated" or "not_run"), range (the estimated range in map units), floor, k_needed, moran and moran_floor (the two Moran's I tests, each with I, z and a one-sided p), reason and unit; gp_adequacy: a list with status (see Details), frac_below (the share of length-scale draws below gp_ell_min), identified and identified_by ("spatial_share" or "length_scale", the rule that decided it; see Details), contraction (one minus the ratio of posterior to prior variance, per length-scale, negative when the posterior is the wider of the two) and prior_gap (the largest gap between the posterior's and the prior's distribution functions, per length-scale; both NA for a length-scale prior this function did not set), spatial_share and sdgp (2.5, 50 and 97.5 percent quantiles; the share only for a gaussian or lognormal family), effective_range (the posterior effective range per axis in map units, same quantiles), residual_moran (the test on the residuals the status rests on: I, z, a one-sided p and k, the number of neighbours; absent when it could not be run, and residual_untested then says why), resolution, unit and prior_mass_below; b_prior: the slope prior brms used ("(flat)" for its default, NA for a model with no slopes), and b_prior_source: where it came from; predictor_levels: the levels each factor or character predictor has in the training rows, which predict() holds new data to; gp_S: the pooled centred range brms::gp(c = ) multiplies; gp_cmeans: the column means brms centred the scaled coordinates on; gp_xy_range: the training extrema of the scaled coordinates, which predict() uses, with gp_S and gp_cmeans, to hold the GP boundary at its fitted value; gp_lengthscale_bounds: the c(lower, upper) the length-scale prior was calibrated over; gp_lscale_prior: the length-scale prior brms::validate_prior() reports the model will actually use, which is not necessarily the one this function requested (several entries, semicolon-separated, if brms resolved the axes differently); loo, looic, convergence_ok (TRUE or FALSE, and NA when nothing was checked, as under check_convergence = FALSE), convergence_diagnostics: n_divergent, n_max_treedepth, ebfmi (per chain), max_rhat, min_neff_ratio, min_ess (the smallest bulk or tail effective sample size) and ess_required (100 per chain), and rhat_failed / neff_failed / ess_failed, the parameters that failed each check by name with their values (R-hat, ESS ratio and ESS; empty when none failed), which is what makes a failed check actionable, rhat_caution, the parameters whose R-hat is between 1.01 and 1.05 with enough effective draws, which do not fail the verdict, plus gp_lscale_below_resolution and gp_adequacy, the share and status described under Details; and n_dropped: the rows prep_model_data() removed for missing or non-finite values or a bad geometry, so $n can be read against nrow(data_sf)). The raw brmsfit is in $engine.

Details

The fitted length-scale is an estimate of how far the spatial dependence reaches only when its posterior sits clear of both that floor and its prior. $info$gp_adequacy says whether it does, and when it does $info$gp_adequacy$effective_range holds the posterior effective range per axis in map units (the raw lscale draws are in per-axis standardised units and are not a distance).

Choose it over fit_gwr_model() when you want one global relationship plus an explicit spatial random field, and uncertainty you can defend; choose GWR instead when the question is how a coefficient varies across the map. Choose fit_rf_model() when predictive accuracy matters more than an interpretable model and the response is non-linear in the predictors. The cost here is time: this is full MCMC via 'brms' and Stan, so it is minutes rather than seconds, and the GP is fitted through a reduced-rank basis approximation whose size (gp_k) trades fidelity against runtime.

GP basis count and boundary factor. brms::gp() builds a full tensor grid over its covariates, so a term gp(..x, ..y, k = gp_k) carries gp_k^2 basis functions: the gp_k argument is the count per dimension, not the total rank. Both gp_k and gp_c are therefore chosen from the ratio of the estimated length-scale to the domain extent, following Riutort-Mayol et al. (2023): gp_c is set large enough to contain the upper length-scale bound, and gp_k large enough to resolve the lower one. The derived value depends on the layout, not on n: 23 on a uniform square, 27 to 38 on the census tracts of Iowa, North Carolina and Texas, and the cap of 50 on California's, whose tracts are clustered.

The domain extent used is the one brms::gp(c = ) itself multiplies: the full pooled range of the column-centred coordinates (brms:::choose_L(), taken over the unique coordinate rows, because brms:::.data_gp() reduces the covariates to unique rows first under the default gr = TRUE, so repeat visits to one location do not widen the domain), not the per-axis half-range in which Riutort-Mayol et al. state their inequalities. Both constraints are really constraints on the boundary \(L = c \times S\), so expressing them in brms's units is what keeps gp_c, gp_k and $info$gp_ell_min describing the basis brms actually builds. A gp_c derived on the half-range convention and handed to brms::gp() produces a boundary twice as wide as intended, against which gp_k under-resolves by a factor of two.

The GP term is built with scale = FALSE. brms::gp() otherwise rescales its covariates so the maximum Euclidean distance between two points is 1, and reports lscale in that space; since this function already standardises the coordinates, and the length-scale prior, gp_c and the adequacy check below are all expressed in those standardised units, a second normalisation would leave every length-scale quantity in the wrong units.

What the basis resolves. The smallest length-scale the chosen basis can resolve is 1.75 * gp_c * S / gp_k, stored in standardised units as $info$gp_ell_min. As an effective range (the distance at which the squared-exponential correlation has fallen to 5 percent, 2.45 length-scales) and in map units it is $info$gp_resolution, one value per axis because each coordinate is divided by its own standard deviation. The floor is soft: the basis keeps 99 percent of a process's variance at the floor, 69 percent at half of it and 41 percent at a third. The default length-scale prior is what makes it bind, with 1 percent of its mass below the floor and about one part in a hundred million below half of it.

Three checks hold the basis against the data.

  1. Before anything is compiled, the autocorrelation range of the response (of its OLS residuals when there are predictors) is estimated with estimate_sac_range() and compared with the coarser axis's floor. That range is a variogram estimate and can be wrong in both directions, so a range below the floor raises a warning only when two other things agree with it. The same variable is autocorrelated at short range (Moran's I over 4 nearest neighbours, one-sided, at 5 percent): a variogram fitted to a response with no spatial structure can still return a short range (in 3 of 60 white-noise draws; estimate_sac_range() refuses most such layers itself). And it is no longer autocorrelated at the floor's distance (Moran's I over the pairs 0.75 to 1.25 floors apart is not both above 0.05, the correlation that defines an effective range, and significant at 5 percent): a variogram can also return a short range for a surface that is smooth over long distances. The warning has class spatialkit_gp_resolution, gives both numbers and the basis size that would resolve the range, says that it is an estimate which the check after sampling tests against the residuals of the fitted model, and says when the basis size is past the cap or past the number of rows, where kriging is the better tool if the range is right. A short range the floor-distance test contradicts is logged and shown by print() without a warning: it can still mean short-range structure beside a longer one, which the basis counts as noise. Nothing before sampling separates the two; the residuals after it do (the third check). A range that cannot be estimated is logged with the reason and shown by print(); the result is in $info$gp_prefit. In 60 simulated draws each (400 points on a 100 km square, floor 33 km) the warning was raised for 59 fields with a range of 8 to 15 km; for 0 or 1 fields that were squared-exponential with a range of 60 or 90 km, a sine or a plane; for 2 of white noise; and for 5 exponential fields with a 60 km range. An exponential field has structure at every scale, and a fit of one with a 50 km range had 62 percent of its length-scale draws below the floor, so those 5 are not plainly wrong.

  2. Also before sampling, the share of the length-scale prior below the floor is computed ($info$gp_adequacy$prior_mass_below). A derived basis keeps it near 0.01; a small gp_k does not (0.98 at gp_k = 6 where the derived value is 23), and a share above 0.10 is logged and flagged by print().

  3. After sampling, under check_convergence = TRUE, the posterior and the residuals are read. The posterior says whether the Gaussian process carries a share of the variance and where its length-scale sits against the floor. It cannot say what the surface left behind, so the residuals are tested for autocorrelation at short range in every fit (Moran's I over 4 nearest neighbours, one-sided, at 5 percent; $info$gp_adequacy$residual_moran). $info$gp_adequacy$status is one of:

    "ok"

    The Gaussian process carries a share of the variance, its length-scale is clear of the floor, and the residuals show no autocorrelation at short range. A surface smoother than the prior expects (a plane, a range longer than the extent) is "ok": its length-scale posterior sits on the long side of the prior and is wider than it.

    "below_resolution"

    The Gaussian process carries a share of the variance and more than 10 percent of the length-scale draws fall below the floor. The 10 percent trigger is this package's operationalisation of the check Riutort-Mayol et al. recommend, not a figure from the paper.

    "unresolved_short_range"

    The residuals are autocorrelated at short range: the signature of structure finer than the basis, counted as noise. It is reached two ways, and $info$gp_adequacy$identified says which. The Gaussian process carries no variance that can be told from zero (FALSE): all of the structure is below the floor. Or it carries a share and its length-scale is clear of the floor (TRUE): it fitted a surface, and finer structure sits beside it, as with a regional trend plus short-range structure.

    "no_signal_above_floor"

    The Gaussian process carries no variance that can be told from zero, and the residuals show nothing left over. A response with no spatial structure gives this, so it is not a failure by itself.

    "not_checked"

    check_convergence = FALSE.

    The second and third raise a warning of class spatialkit_gp_adequacy; the fourth is logged. When the residuals cannot be tested (an ordinal or categorical family has no residual per row; a posterior that cannot be drawn), the status rests on the posterior alone, a line is logged, the reason is in $info$gp_adequacy$residual_untested, and print() keeps its flag on a variogram range that was below the floor.

    The residual test rests on fits of points on a 100 km square whose
floor is 32 to 33 km.  Sampled fits: ten of a response with a
component below the floor (a field with an 8 or 12 km range, alone or
beside a plane or a field with a 90 km range) had p of 5.3e-10 to
0.014, and five of the ten had a posterior that reads \code{"ok"};
twelve of a response with none (planes, bowls, a sine, fields with
ranges of 45 to 200 km) had p of 0.66 to 0.97.  At the posterior mode
of the same model, computed without sampling, the test was
significant in 0 of 160 fits of fields with ranges of 45 to 200 km
and in 3 of 120 fits of a plane, a bowl and a sine (one noise draw of
the 40, shared by the three, whose own Moran's I has p = 0.003);
and in 16 to 18 of 20 fits of each of four responses with an 8 km
field in them, where the length-scale at the mode was below the floor
in 0 or 1 of the 20.  On a fit with nothing left over the test is
conservative, because the surface takes up part of the noise and
leaves the residuals slightly negatively autocorrelated (median I of
-0.03 to -0.07).  It is not sharp just below the floor: a field with
a 20 km range was significant in 8 of 20 fits, and there it is the
length-scale draws that report it (\code{"below_resolution"}).  An
exponential field has structure at every scale and can be reported
with a range above the floor (8 of 20 fits at 60 km).  The 5 percent
level is the usual one and is not tuned; with many rows a small
leftover autocorrelation is significant, so read the size of I
beside its p.

"No variance
that can be told from zero" is decided on the Gaussian process's share
of the variance, \code{sdgp^2 / (sdgp^2 + sigma^2)}: its 2.5 percent
quantile is under 0.01.  On nine fits that quantile was 0.000 to 0.003
for the three with nothing for the process to find and 0.17 to 0.94
for the six with a surface; the threshold rests on those nine.  It
does not mark off a response whose structure is all below the floor:
on five fits of a field with an 8 km range under a 33 km floor the
quantile was 0.000, 0.000, 0.001, 0.015 and 0.019, so two of the five
count as carrying a share, and it is the residual test that reports
them.  The
share exists for a gaussian or lognormal family.  For any other
family the length-scales decide instead: the process is not identified
when on every axis the posterior kept more than three quarters of its
prior's variance and the largest gap between its distribution function
and the prior's is under 0.30.  That second rule has been checked on
the length-scale draws of the same nine gaussian fits, where it agrees
with the share on eight, and on no fit of another family.
\code{$info$gp_adequacy$identified_by} says which rule was used.  The width of the length-scale posterior does not
decide by itself, because a posterior that moved to longer
length-scales is wider than its prior; and the share of draws below
the floor cannot detect an unidentified process, because a posterior
the data did not move puts 1 percent below the floor, the same as the
prior.

A response whose range is below the floor needs a finer basis and a prior that allows the shorter length-scale, both of which gp_resolution sets, up to the cap. Past the cap this model is the wrong tool: resolving a 30 km range on the North Carolina tracts would take 156 functions per dimension, 24,336 in all for 2,672 points. Kriging has no such floor; see kriging_adequacy() for cell means.

Coordinate scaling and anisotropy. Before fitting the GP, X and Y coordinates are each centred and divided by their own standard deviation. This is a conditioning step: easting and northing frequently span very different ranges in a projected CRS, and handing Stan raw metres samples poorly.

Because the axes are scaled independently, a single shared length-scale in the scaled space corresponds to an anisotropic kernel in the original CRS, stretched by whatever ratio sd(X)/sd(Y) happens to take. That ratio is a property of how the sampling locations are laid out, not of the process being modelled, so it is not a defensible source of anisotropy.

gp_iso = FALSE (the default) therefore fits one length-scale per axis, letting the model estimate directional structure from the data instead of inheriting it from the standardisation. Set gp_iso = TRUE to recover the previous single-length-scale behaviour.

gp_iso does not affect cost: brms::gp() builds a tensor grid either way, so the model carries gp_k^2 basis functions regardless. The stored $info$coord_scaling list records the scaling strategy, and $info$gp_iso records which kernel was used.

Warnings

Every warning this function raises carries a condition class, so a caller can catch or muffle exactly one of them by name:

spatialkit_rows_dropped, spatialkit_constant_predictor

From prep_model_data(): incomplete rows were dropped, with the counts; a predictor takes one value in every row kept.

spatialkit_gp_basis_size

Fewer than one row per ten basis functions.

spatialkit_gp_resolution

A variogram fitted before compiling puts the response's range below what the basis resolves, and the autocorrelation of the response agrees. An estimate; the check after sampling tests it against the residuals of the fitted model.

spatialkit_convergence

The sampler's diagnostics fail.

spatialkit_gp_adequacy

The basis is too coarse for the data: the posterior asks for a shorter length-scale than it resolves ("below_resolution"), or the residuals are autocorrelated at short range ("unresolved_short_range").

A response that takes a single value is an error, raised before anything is compiled. The convergence warning carries the checks that failed as failed ("divergent", "ebfmi", "rhat", "ess"). cv_bayes() fits once per fold; it collects the last four classes from its folds and raises each once for the run, naming the folds, and cv_spatial() does the same for a fit_fn that calls this function.

Non-Gaussian responses

Nothing in this function is Gaussian-specific except its default. A numeric count, binary (0/1 or logical) or bounded response passes straight through to brms under the family you name; zero-inflated and hurdle counts, negative binomial, Bernoulli, beta, ordinal, categorical and mixture families have all been verified to reach brms::brm() with the GP term intact, the length-scale prior attached to each distributional parameter's GP.

The response check is family-aware. A factor or character response is accepted only under brms::categorical() or an ordinal family (cumulative, sratio, cratio, acat), and refused under every other family before anything is compiled; under gaussian a logical response is refused too. The case to watch is a two-level factor under brms::bernoulli(): brms would fit it, but residuals(), summary(), model_metrics() and cv_bayes() could not score a factor, so convert it to 0/1 first.

An ordinal or categorical fit has a probability per response category, not one expected value per row. predict() with its default type = "epred", fitted(), residuals(), summary() and model_metrics() therefore stop with a message saying so, and cv_bayes() refuses the family before fitting anything. predict(type = "predict", draws = TRUE) returns the posterior predicted categories, as category indices, for new rows as well as the training ones (the share of draws in each category estimates its probability), and brms::posterior_epred(fit$engine) the probabilities for the training rows.

For the numeric families two things follow. First, the metrics that come back from model_metrics() and the cv_*() functions are not all meaningful for such a response: RMSE and MAE are, MAPE, SMAPE and R-squared are Gaussian-shaped, and for this backend cv_bayes()'s CRPS and interval coverage are the proper scores to read. See model_metrics(), section "Which metrics survive a non-Gaussian response". Second, estimate_sac_range() fits a variogram to the raw response (or OLS residuals), whose variance tracks its mean for a count; the range it reports is then less trustworthy than for a Gaussian response, and its help page says how.

One trap. The response check reads the family's name through brms's own accessor; a family object it cannot name is treated as unknown and the check is skipped entirely, without falling back to either rule above. A malformed family therefore buys less validation, not more, and a wrong response type will surface as a Stan error, with no message from this function.

Spatial confounding

A fixed-effect coefficient estimated alongside a spatial random effect is a different quantity from the same coefficient in a non-spatial fit. When a covariate is itself spatially smooth, the GP term absorbs part of its effect and the two estimates can disagree sharply; when the response is smoother than the covariate, the estimate can shrink toward zero regardless of the true effect (Bolin and Wallin 2025). Under a correctly specified spatial model this is not a bias but a change of estimand (Zimmerman and Ver Hoef 2022): the spatial coefficient is the effect net of whatever the spatial field can explain, and the non-spatial one is not. Which of the two a user wants depends on the question, so the honest diagnostic is to report both side by side and leave them unadjusted: fit the same formula with stats::lm() or stats::glm() and compare. Compare like with like: under standardize_predictors = TRUE the coefficients here are per standard deviation of each predictor, so either fit the non-spatial model on the same standardised columns or divide these slopes by $info$predictor_scaling[[name]]$scale first (see coef.bayesian_fit).

The literature on remedies is unsettled and this function takes no side. Restricted spatial regression (Hughes and Haran 2013) projects the spatial effect off the covariate space; later work argues it does not deliver what it promises (Hanks et al. 2015; Khan and Calder 2022). Within this backend, modelling the covariate and the spatial field as explicitly correlated (Marques, Kneib and Klein 2022) is expressible in a brms formula with no new code, and a spectral adjustment (Guan et al. 2023) is the principled route a Hilbert-space basis is well placed to support later.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# Not run: fits with Stan, which needs a working C++ toolchain and takes
# minutes of MCMC -- both outside what an example may assume.
if (requireNamespace("brms", quietly = TRUE)) {
  library(sf)
  set.seed(1)
  n <- 60
  dat <- st_as_sf(
    data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000),
               elev = rnorm(n)),
    coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
  )
  dat$price <- 10 + 0.01 * (st_coordinates(dat)[, 1] - 5e5) +
    2 * dat$elev + rnorm(n)
  # Two short chains keep this to a few minutes; expect Stan to warn about
  # effective sample size, which is the cost of that.  Use its defaults
  # (chains = 4, iter = 2000) for a fit to report.
  fit <- fit_bayesian_spatial_model(dat, "price", "elev",
                                    chains = 2, iter = 1000,
                                    compute_loo = FALSE)
  print(summary(fit))
  head(predict(fit, newdata = dat))

  # A zero-inflated count.  The family is the only thing that changes.
  # summary()'s R2 and MAPE assume a Gaussian response, so for a count
  # read the coefficients here and score the model with cv_bayes(), whose
  # CRPS and interval coverage are defined for any response.
  dat$count <- rpois(n, exp(0.5 + 0.8 * dat$elev)) * rbinom(n, 1, 0.7)
  fit_zip <- fit_bayesian_spatial_model(dat, "count", "elev",
                                        family = brms::zero_inflated_poisson(),
                                        chains = 2, iter = 1000,
                                        compute_loo = FALSE)
  coef(fit_zip)
}
} # }
